visible.name: Tessa Marlowe
visible.line: Tessa Marlowe, 26, is the cofounder and CEO of a three-person climate hardware startup in a shared garage workshop, selling a countertop dryer that turns kitchen scraps into dry, odorless soil amendment.

project.title: Loam
project.logline: A countertop appliance that dries and sterilizes food scraps overnight into a compost-ready powder; forty hand-built units are with users and 1,900 people are on the waitlist.
constraints: Pre-seed runway is eleven months at the current burn of 27,000 dollars a month.
The enclosure supplier needs a minimum order of 500 units for any custom tooling.
Safety certification is required before any retailer will stock the unit, and the test lab has a ten-week queue.
The team is three people: Tessa, a cofounder who owns firmware, and a part-time contractor for assembly.
The first production batch must ship before the end of the quarter to honor the preorder promise.

tone_requests.text: Give me the answer first, then the reason, in under 100 words unless I ask for more.
Challenge my numbers instead of agreeing with them.
No startup clichés: hustle, disrupt, unlock, supercharge.
When it is a decision, give me a recommendation and the one risk that could make it wrong.
Skip the pep talk; I know how tight the runway is.
Use my own numbers back to me so I know you read them.

stated_views.text: Most founders talk to too few users and ship too late.
A product page that explains too much is a product page that is hiding something.
Preorders are the only honest survey.
Polish is something you earn after people pay.
Speed of learning is the real moat for a three-person team.

plans.text: On Day 3 I'm sending the monthly investor update to our eleven backers.
On Day 6 I'm shipping the first hundred preorders and filming the packing line.
On Day 10 I'm presenting to a climate accelerator panel for twenty minutes.

taste_ab.prompt: A product page needs a hero photo. What goes up?
options: A phone photo of the unit on a real counter
A studio shot with controlled light

taste_ab.prompt: A harsh one-star review appears under the product. What happens?
options: Write privately to the reviewer and let the review stand
Reply publicly within the hour and offer a fix

taste_ab.prompt: A creator asks for a free review unit.
options: Send one with a tracking link
Send one only if you have seen their work

taste_ab.prompt: A returned unit comes back in good shape. What now?
options: Take it apart and rebuild it before it goes anywhere
Resell it as refurbished at a discount

taste_ab.prompt: Should there be an accessory bundle at checkout?

new_work.text: Here's my draft investor update subject and first lines: "Loam, March: 212 preorders, 9 percent conversion, 3 refund requests." I run it the same day every month. Is the opening doing its job, or is it too much like a spreadsheet?

I just finished eight user calls about our countertop food-scrap dryer. Five said the noise during the overnight cycle is the first thing they notice, two want a smaller bin, and one said she would pay double for it to be silent. How should I synthesize this for the team?

I'm writing the pitch narrative for a pre-seed meeting on Friday. The company turns kitchen scraps into dry, odorless soil amendment on the counter. Should it open with the preorder numbers or with the story of why I built it?
I need a job post for our first hardware engineer. We're three people in a garage with forty hand-built units out. I have it down to five lines with a salary. Does that sound right or too thin?
Our launch plan is a Tuesday in three weeks with a mailing list of 1,900, a small forum post and four creators. Should I add a launch discount for the first two hundred buyers, and how big?
I'm designing the pricing page. We've tested 249, 279 and 299 dollars; 279 converted best at 9.1 percent but 299 had fewer refund requests. Which should I go live with?
The supplier says tooling for the enclosure will take eleven weeks and cost 38,000 dollars. A stock enclosure lets us ship 500 units next month. What would you do?
A customer emailed that the lid rattles during the dry cycle. I've seen it in three units. How should I reply today, and do I pause shipments?
I'm choosing packaging for the first 500 units. A plain printed recycled box costs 1.20 dollars a unit and a rigid box with an insert costs 4.10. Margin is thin. Which one?
We need a refund policy for the preorder page. I'm leaning toward thirty days, no questions asked, since that's what built trust in our first forty units. What are the risks?

I have to cut two of five features from the next firmware release because we have one week. The ones in question are a scheduling app, a bin-full alert, a quiet mode, a pause button and a firmware self-update. Which two?

I'm writing the waitlist email announcing the ship date slipping by two weeks because of a part shortage. I want it short and plain. Here's my draft: "Heads up: shipping moves to May 20. Thanks for your patience." Is that enough?
A reporter at a climate newsletter asked for a demo unit and an interview. Our cofounder wants to wait until the next firmware is out. Should I say yes now?
We've got an offer from a retailer for 300 units on consignment at 40 percent. We've sold only direct so far. Should I take it, and what would I ask for?
I'm preparing a public roadmap post. It lists six items and I want users to vote. Should I post it now or wait until we fix the noise issue?
I need to rewrite the product's quick-start card. Right now it has nine steps and three photos. Customers keep skipping step six. How do I shorten it?
Our first batch had a 2 percent defect rate on the heating element. Should I recall, replace on request, or just fix it in the second batch?
I'm drafting a thank-you note to the first hundred buyers. I'd like it to ask for a one-line review and one photo. Does asking for both feel greedy?
My cofounder wants to hire a brand designer for a full identity. I want to keep the one-hour logo and spend the money on a second prototype. How do we settle this?
I've got a two-minute demo video script: unboxing, scraps in, overnight cycle, dry soil out. I'd like it to feel lived-in rather than polished. What would you change?
A pilot with a community garden wants 20 units at cost. It'd teach us a lot about outdoor use but costs us about 3,000 dollars. Do I do it?
I'm choosing between selling at a Saturday farmers market and running a small ad test. I have 800 dollars this month. Which one?
Here's the one-slide traction summary for the deck: preorders by week, repeat orders, refund rate. Is there a better chart than three small line graphs?
I need to tell our supplier we're switching to a second one because they missed a delivery. I'd like to be direct but keep the relationship. Here's my draft message. How do I fix the tone?
I'm writing my answer to the question "why will you win?" for an accelerator form. Limit 100 words. My current draft leans on speed. Is that enough?
Planning the next two-week cycle: a card with four items — fix lid rattle, ship 100 preorders, test a quieter fan, interview five more users. Is that too much for a team of three?

hand_written: Development personas only: written by hand (Claude, as the build worker), not by a Muse Spark call. The final lives' taste_ab items come from the isolated Muse Spark call (5.1).
